subject: orthopaedics
title: Peripheral nerve injuries: classify, localise, time repair

steps.tx: **Neuropraxia** blocks conduction without cutting the axon, and recovery returns within weeks as myelin repairs. In **axonotmesis** the axon divides but the sheath survives, so regrowth follows the tube at about a millimetre each day. **Neurotmesis** divides the whole nerve and needs surgical repair for useful recovery. An advancing Tinel sign suggests regrowth, while a static sign suggests failure.
steps.say: The mildest injury blocks the signal while the nerve fibre itself stays intact. Recovery then returns over weeks as the insulating layer repairs itself. A deeper injury cuts the fibre but leaves its guiding tube in place. Regrowth travels slowly along that tube toward the target muscle. Complete division of the whole nerve needs surgical joining for useful recovery.

vis.alt: Diagram illustrating Sunderland's five degrees of nerve injury, from neuropraxia to neurotmesis, showing damage to nerve sheaths and axons.
vis.caption: Sunderland classification of peripheral nerve injury. Image: Davplast, CC BY-SA 4.0, Wikimedia Commons.

steps.tx: An **axillary nerve** injury flattens the deltoid and causes numbness over the regimental badge area after shoulder injury. A **radial nerve** injury in the spiral groove causes wrist drop, classically after sleeping with the arm draped, the Saturday night palsy. Triceps power stays normal in a groove lesion, while finger drop alone suggests a **posterior interosseous** lesion. A cock up splint supports the hand during recovery.
steps.say: A shoulder injury can damage the nerve that lifts the arm sideways. Loss of that muscle flattens the normal rounded contour of the shoulder. Pressure on the upper arm nerve during deep sleep can paralyse wrist extension. The hand then hangs limply because the extensor muscles lose their signal. A splint holds the wrist up while the nerve recovers slowly.

steps.tx: This photograph shows a clear **wrist drop** with the hand hanging limp, and the inset marks the **spiral groove** level on the humerus. That level localises a **radial nerve** lesion, where triceps power usually survives. The image matters because posture alone can point to the nerve before formal testing begins. For the exam, connect this Saturday night pattern with a cock up splint and watchful recovery.
steps.say: The photograph shows a hand that hangs downward because extension has failed completely. An inset bone diagram will mark the groove where the nerve winds around the upper arm. Injury at that groove explains weakness below it while the elbow extensor still works. This visible posture lets you name the injured nerve within seconds. Examiners use this picture because localisation follows directly from the anatomy shown.

vis.alt: Side view of drooping wrist and hand plus humerus inset marking spiral groove level.
vis.caption: Clinical photo showing wrist drop from radial nerve palsy. Illustration: StewardMD original.

steps.tx: A **median nerve** injury wastes the thenar muscles and makes the hand look like a benediction when the patient tries a fist. Failure of the OK sign points to an **anterior interosseous** lesion of the deep branch. **Carpal tunnel** disease wakes the patient at night and improves with shaking the hand, the flick sign. An ulnar injury claws the fingers and makes the Froment sign positive.
steps.say: Damage to one hand nerve will waste the fleshy muscle at the thumb base. The patient then fails to pinch a sheet of paper firmly between fingers. Night pain and tingling in the hand suggest compression inside the wrist tunnel. Shaking the hand often relieves that night discomfort for a short time. Damage to the other main hand nerve will curl the fingers into a claw.

steps.tx: An **Erb palsy** from a C5 and C6 injury leaves the arm in the waiter tip posture with weak shoulder and elbow. A **Klumpke palsy** from C8 and T1 injury claws the hand and may add a Horner syndrome. A common peroneal injury at the fibular neck causes **foot drop** and a high steppage gait. Early repair or grafting within months gives the best chance of recovery.
steps.say: Upper root injury leaves the arm hanging with the palm turned backward. The shoulder and elbow lose most of their useful power in that pattern. Lower root injury will instead weaken the small muscles inside the hand itself. Pressure where the leg nerve winds around the fibular neck will drop the foot. The patient will then lift the knee high so the toes clear the ground.
